summary: The altimeter is a barometer: what it reads depends on the pressure you set. QNH gives altitude (amsl) for terrain, QFE gives height above the aerodrome for the circuit, and 1013 gives flight levels for separation. En route below 3,000 ft use the Regional Pressure Setting, the lowest forecast QNH for each hour in your Altimeter Setting Region. Above the transition altitude (3,000 ft over most of the UK) use flight levels; under a TMA use an aerodrome QNH from beneath it. Flying into low pressure or cold air puts you lower than indicated: high to low, beware below. Semicircular levels go by magnetic track: east odd, west even, VFR plus 500.
sections: How the altimeter works
Pressure falls as you climb. The altimeter is a barometer with its scale marked in feet instead of pressure

Static pressure from the static vent fills the sealed instrument case. Inside is an aneroid capsule: sealed, with most of the air removed and a spring stopping it collapsing. As you climb, static pressure falls, the capsule expands, and linkage and gearing turn the pointers (the textbook simplifies this as "a fixed amount of air in the capsule")
Three pointers: 100 ft, 1,000 ft and 10,000 ft. A striped sector shows when you are below 10,000 ft
The subscale knob sets the datum pressure, shown in the pressure window. The altimeter reads height or altitude above whatever pressure level is set
Units: hectopascals (hPa) replaced millibars in the UK on 17 November 2011. 1 hPa = 1 mb
Below 5,000 ft, 1 hPa is roughly 30 ft
QNH, QFE and standard pressure
QNH: mean sea level pressure. The altimeter reads altitude, above mean sea level (amsl). Use it for terrain and obstacles, because charts give elevations amsl
QNH changes with time and place, so keep updating it as the day goes on and as you fly from region to region

QFE: the pressure at aerodrome elevation (the highest point on the landing area). The altimeter reads height above aerodrome level (aal), so a 1,000 ft circuit shows 1,000 ft. Common for take-off, circuits and landing
ATC pass QFE changes. Different aerodromes have different QFEs, depending on elevation and the pressure pattern
Standard pressure: 1013.2 hPa (1013). The altimeter reads pressure altitude; drop the last two zeros for a flight level (PA 3,500 ft = FL35)
1013 is used for vertical separation between aircraft on the same setting, at higher levels where terrain is no longer the concern, and saves updating QNH
Example, high-pressure day (QNH 1030, aerodrome 1,500 ft, QFE 980): an aircraft at 4,000 ft altitude is at FL35 on 1013 and 2,500 ft height on QFE
Altimeter Setting Regions and the RPS
The UK is divided into 20 Altimeter Setting Regions (ASRs). Everyone on the same region's setting has the same datum, which keeps them vertically separated
The Regional Pressure Setting (RPS, often called the regional QNH) is the lowest forecast QNH in the region for each hour, so you are at, or slightly above, the altitude shown
No aerodrome QNH in the region should be lower than the RPS
ATS update the RPS every hour. Change it when you cross into another region

The ASR chart is in the UK AIP (ENR 6). Names: Portree, Skerry, Belfast, Holyhead, Scillies, Shetland, Orkney, Marlin, Petrel, Rattray, Tyne, Skua, Puffin, Barnsley, Humber, Wessex, Cotswold, Chatham, Portland, Yarmouth
Ask for it by name: "Chatham regional pressure setting"
Transition altitude, layer and level
Transition altitude (TA): at and below it, vertical position is controlled by altitude on QNH. It is 3,000 ft amsl over most of the UK; exceptions under some controlled airspace are in AIP ENR 1.7
Above TA you use flight levels on 1013: all aircraft in controlled airspace, and above 3,000 ft outside it (subject to the AIP's exceptions)
Transition level (TL): the lowest flight level available above the transition altitude. The space between TA and TL is the transition layer
Climbing through TA, give your position as a flight level; descending through TL, give it as an altitude
Flight plans: altitudes below TA, flight levels above TL
Pick a cruising level that clears terrain, meets any ATS requirement, and follows the semicircular rule where it applies
A typical cross-country
Most PPL cross-countries stay outside controlled airspace and below 3,000 ft amsl
In the circuit, at either end: aerodrome QFE (height aal) or aerodrome QNH (altitude), as you prefer
En route: the Regional Pressure Setting, so the altimeter shows altitude amsl
Take-off and climb
Two useful readings: height aal on QFE (for the circuit) and altitude on QNH (for terrain, obstacles and airspace)
Inside controlled airspace: take off on aerodrome QNH or QFE. With two altimeters, set one to aerodrome QNH (the other to QNH or QFE)
Climb on aerodrome QNH up to the TA, reporting altitude. Once cleared above the TA and climbing, report a flight level, provided you are no more than 2,000 ft below the TA (unless ATC ask otherwise)
Outside controlled airspace: QNH or QFE for take-off and climb; report altitude. Under IFR, report a flight level once through the TA
Departing from under a TMA or CTA: use aerodrome QNH below the TA beneath it. QFE may still be used in the circuit
En route: high to low, beware below
Update the RPS periodically and whenever you enter a new region
Flying into lower pressure with the old setting, the altimeter over-reads: you gradually descend while it shows the same figure
E.g. cruising at 1,000 ft on 1020 into an area where the QNH is 1010: the 1020 level is about 300 ft below sea level, so you are really at about 700 ft
Colder air is denser, so a pressure level is lower in cold air than warm. Flying from warm to cold, you descend in real terms
In very cold air you can be up to about 10% lower than indicated. Still fly by the altimeter, but allow for it
"High to low, beware below": applies to both low pressure and low temperature
Choosing a flight level when the QNH is low
When QNH is below 1013, the 1013 hPa level is below sea level, so a flight level is lower than its number suggests
QNH 996: 17 hPa × 30 ft ≈ 500 ft. FL40 is only about 3,500 ft amsl
Traffic at 3,000 ft would be only 500 ft below you at FL40; a 2,800 ft hill only 700 ft below
To be 1,000 ft above something at 3,000 ft amsl that day, the lowest suitable level is FL45 (about 4,000 ft amsl)
Quick conversion: altitude ≈ flight level × 100 + (QNH − 1013) × 30 ft
Inside controlled airspace
Above 3,000 ft amsl or the TA, whichever is higher, en-route aircraft fly flight levels on 1013
The RPS goes on the second altimeter en route for checking terrain clearance
In a CTR or TMA, at or below the TA, ATC give you the QNH in your clearance to enter
Outside controlled airspace
At or below 3,000 ft amsl: the RPS, or the QNH of an aerodrome nearby
Beneath a TMA or CTA: the QNH of an aerodrome under it. It is what the traffic above is using, and stops you climbing into the airspace by mistake if it differs from the RPS
MATZ penetration: normally the aerodrome QFE. In a combined MATZ (CMATZ) you get the lowest of its QFEs, the clutch QFE. Sometimes QNH is given instead. CAP 413 has the procedure
Report vertical position as altitude. On an advisory route at or below 3,000 ft, use the RPS
IFR in level flight above 3,000 ft (or the TA if higher): 1013 set, semicircular levels, report flight levels; RPS for terrain checks
VFR above 3,000 ft may stay on the RPS (useful with changing headings and heights). Semicircular levels are not required, but if you choose them you must set 1013
The semicircular rule
Separates traffic going opposite ways. Required for IFR; strongly recommended for VFR
Based on magnetic track, not heading: in a strong crosswind, fast and slow aircraft on the same track have different headings
Track 000°–179° (eastbound): IFR at odd thousands (FL30, FL50, FL70); VFR at odd + 500 (FL35, FL55, FL75)
Track 180°–359° (westbound): IFR at even thousands (FL40, FL60); VFR at even + 500 (FL45, FL65)
Memory aid: east is odd, west is even; VFR adds 500
Common trap: a question gives a heading. The rule uses track; with no wind information, treat the heading as the track
Approach, landing and missed approach
Descending from a flight level to an altitude, ATC pass the aerodrome QNH. It may differ slightly from the RPS but should never be lower
Set QNH as you leave your cruising level, unless more flight-level reports are wanted (then set it after the last one)
Stay on aerodrome QNH until approaching the circuit or established on final, then QFE if you wish
Radar approach: the controller assumes QNH and gives altitudes, with a reminder in the phraseology. Tell them if you are on QFE and they will give heights instead. QNH is recommended
Landing beneath a TMA or CTA: aerodrome QNH below the TA; QFE may be used in the circuit
Missed approach: you may keep the final-approach setting, but report altitude on aerodrome QNH unless ATC say otherwise

cards.q: What is the altimeter, really?
cards.a: A barometer (aneroid capsule) with a scale in feet.

cards.q: Below 5,000 ft, 1 hPa is about how many feet?
What does a striped sector on the altimeter show?
QNH set: the altimeter reads?
QFE set: the altimeter reads?
1013 set: the altimeter reads?
cards.a: Pressure altitude, given as a flight level.

cards.q: What is aerodrome elevation?
cards.a: The highest point on the landing area.

cards.q: PA 3,500 ft as a flight level?
How many UK Altimeter Setting Regions?
What is the Regional Pressure Setting?
cards.a: The lowest forecast QNH in the region for each hour.

cards.q: Can an aerodrome QNH be lower than the RPS?
cards.a: It should not be: the RPS is the lowest forecast value.

cards.q: How often is the RPS updated?
Where is the ASR chart?
Usual UK transition altitude?
What is the transition level?
cards.a: The lowest flight level available above the transition altitude.

cards.q: What is the transition layer?
cards.a: The airspace between the transition altitude and the transition level.

cards.q: Climbing through TA, report as?
Descending through TL, report as?
Two altimeters in controlled airspace on take-off?
cards.a: At least one on aerodrome QNH.

cards.q: Departing beneath a TMA, which setting below TA?
cards.a: Aerodrome QNH (QFE allowed in the circuit).

cards.q: En-route setting on a typical VFR cross-country?
Effect of flying into lower pressure without resetting?
Effect of flying into colder air?
cards.a: You are lower than indicated (up to about 10% in very cold air).

cards.q: Memory aid for pressure and temperature errors?
QNH 996: roughly what altitude is FL40?
QNH 996: lowest FL to clear 3,000 ft amsl by 1,000 ft?
Under a TMA outside controlled airspace, which setting?
cards.a: QNH of an aerodrome beneath the TMA.

cards.q: MATZ penetration: usual setting?
cards.a: Aerodrome QFE (clutch QFE in a combined MATZ).

cards.q: What is the clutch QFE?
cards.a: The lowest QFE of the aerodromes in a combined MATZ.

cards.q: VFR above 3,000 ft on semicircular levels: which setting?
Semicircular rule is based on?
VFR, track 000–179°M: which levels?
VFR, track 180–359°M: which levels?
IFR, track 000–179°M: which levels?
Radar approach: which setting does the controller assume?
Missed approach: report vertical position as?
cards.a: Altitude on aerodrome QNH, unless ATC say otherwise.

quiz.q: With QNH set on the subscale, you report vertical position as:
quiz.why: QNH gives altitude amsl. QFE gives height, 1013 gives a flight level, and elevation is a fixed point on the ground, not your level.

quiz.q: The Regional Pressure Setting is:
o: The lowest forecast QNH in the region for each hour
The lowest actual QNH in the region for each hour
The highest forecast QNH in the region for each hour
The average QNH of aerodromes in the region
quiz.why: It is the lowest forecast value, so you are at or slightly above the altitude shown. 'Actual' is the usual trap.

quiz.q: The main purpose of (i) QFE and (ii) QNH is:
o: (i) Height above the aerodrome (ii) terrain and obstacle clearance
(i) Height above the aerodrome (ii) separation from other traffic
(i) Separation from other traffic (ii) terrain clearance
(i) Terrain clearance (ii) height above the aerodrome
quiz.why: QFE tells you your height aal for the circuit; QNH relates you to charted elevations amsl. Separation from other traffic at higher levels is what 1013 is for.

quiz.q: If you don't update the altimeter setting, which is the dangerous direction to fly?
o: High to low pressure, or warmer to colder air
Low to high pressure, or colder to warmer air
High to low pressure, or colder to warmer air
Low to high pressure, or warmer to colder air
quiz.why: Both lower pressure and colder air put you lower than indicated: high to low, beware below. The distractors mix one correct half with one wrong half.

quiz.q: A VFR flight cruising above 3,000 ft amsl:
o: Should consider the semicircular rule as good practice; the lowest westbound level is FL45
Must follow the semicircular rule; the lowest westbound level is FL45
Should consider the semicircular rule; the lowest westbound level is FL35
Must follow the semicircular rule; the lowest westbound level is FL35
quiz.why: For VFR the rule is recommended, not required. Westbound VFR levels are even + 500, so the lowest above 3,000 ft is FL45; FL35 is eastbound.

quiz.q: Flying beneath a TMA outside controlled airspace, which setting should you use?
o: The QNH of an aerodrome beneath the TMA
The QFE of an aerodrome beneath the TMA
Whichever is lower, the RPS or an aerodrome QNH
quiz.why: Use the QNH of an aerodrome under the TMA: it matches the traffic above and protects the TMA base. The RPS may differ slightly.

quiz.q: The transition altitude is:
o: The altitude at and below which vertical position is controlled by reference to altitude on QNH
The altitude above which you must fly a flight level on QFE
The lowest flight level available for cruising
quiz.why: It is defined by QNH and altitude. It is 3,000 ft over most of the UK but not everywhere; the lowest usable flight level is the transition level.

quiz.q: A VFR aircraft is on a magnetic track of 055°. Which semicircular level is correct?
quiz.why: Track 000–179° is odd thousands; VFR adds 500, so FL35, FL55, FL75. FL50 is the IFR level; FL40 and FL45 are westbound.

quiz.q: The semicircular rule is based on:
quiz.why: Magnetic track. In a crosswind two aircraft on the same track can have very different headings.

quiz.q: An IFR flight on a magnetic track of 250°. Which is a correct cruising level?
quiz.why: Westbound IFR flies even thousands (FL40, FL60...). Plus 500 is for VFR; odd thousands are eastbound.

quiz.q: A VFR flight on a magnetic track of 180°. Which level?
quiz.why: 180° is in the westbound half (180–359°), so VFR uses even + 500.

quiz.q: QNH is 996 hPa. Roughly what altitude is FL40?
quiz.why: 17 hPa × 30 ft ≈ 500 ft. The 1013 level is 500 ft below sea level, so FL40 ≈ 3,500 ft. Low QNH makes flight levels lower, not higher.

quiz.q: QNH 996. You need 1,000 ft clearance above traffic at 3,000 ft amsl. Lowest suitable level?
quiz.why: FL45 ≈ 4,000 ft amsl that day. FL40 is only about 3,500 ft, giving 500 ft separation.

quiz.q: Cruising at 1,000 ft with 1020 set, you fly into an area where the QNH is 1010. Your actual altitude is about:
quiz.why: The 1020 level is about 300 ft below sea level there (10 × 30 ft), so 1,000 ft above it is about 700 ft amsl.

quiz.q: In very cold air, how much lower than indicated could you be?
o: Not at all if QNH is correct
quiz.why: Cold dense air lowers the pressure levels; the error can reach about 10% even with the correct QNH set.

quiz.q: The transition level is:
o: The lowest flight level available above the transition altitude
The highest altitude at which QNH is used
The level at which QFE changes to QNH
quiz.why: TL is a flight level, the first usable one above TA; between them is the transition layer.

quiz.q: Climbing through the transition altitude, you give your vertical position as:
quiz.why: Climbing, change to flight levels at TA; descending, change to altitude at TL.

quiz.q: Inside controlled airspace with two altimeters, for take-off you should have:
o: At least one on aerodrome QNH
One on 1013 and one on QFE
quiz.why: One on aerodrome QNH for terrain and traffic; the other on QNH or QFE.

quiz.q: How is the aircraft's vertical position reported outside controlled airspace?
quiz.why: Outside controlled airspace, communications and flight plans use altitude (IFR above the TA excepted).

quiz.q: Crossing a combined MATZ, what setting are you usually given?
o: The clutch QFE: the lowest QFE of the aerodromes
The highest QFE of the aerodromes
quiz.why: The lowest QFE is given, the clutch QFE. Sometimes QNH is passed instead when crossing.

quiz.q: A VFR pilot above 3,000 ft chooses to fly semicircular levels. Which setting?
quiz.why: VFR may stay on the RPS, but semicircular levels are flight levels, so 1013 must be set if you fly them.

quiz.q: How often is the Regional Pressure Setting updated?
o: Only when it changes by 2 hPa
quiz.why: Hourly, as the lowest forecast QNH for each hour.

quiz.q: On a radar approach, which setting does the controller assume you have?
quiz.why: QNH is assumed and altitudes are given. If you say you are on QFE, the controller gives heights instead.

quiz.q: During a missed approach, vertical position should be reported as:
o: Altitude on aerodrome QNH, unless ATC instruct otherwise
quiz.why: You may keep the final-approach setting, but report altitude on aerodrome QNH.

quiz.q: Below 5,000 ft, a 1 hPa change in setting moves the altimeter reading by about:
quiz.why: About 30 ft per hPa low down (often rounded to 27–30 ft).

quiz.q: On a high-pressure day (QNH 1030), an aircraft is at 4,000 ft altitude. Its flight level is about:
quiz.why: QNH is 17 hPa above 1013, so the 1013 level is about 500 ft above sea level, making the aircraft about FL35. High QNH makes the flight level lower than the altitude.

quiz.q: Aerodrome elevation 1,500 ft. With QFE set on the ground, the altimeter reads:
quiz.why: QFE is the pressure at aerodrome level, so on the ground it reads zero. QNH would read 1,500 ft.

quiz.q: Which statement about the RPS and an aerodrome QNH in the same region is right?
o: The aerodrome QNH should not be lower than the RPS
The aerodrome QNH should not be higher than the RPS
The RPS is the aerodrome QNH of the largest airport
quiz.why: The RPS is the lowest forecast QNH, so aerodrome QNHs should be equal or higher.

quiz.q: Outside controlled airspace at or below 3,000 ft amsl, which settings may you use?
o: The RPS or the QNH of an aerodrome nearby
quiz.why: Either the RPS or a nearby aerodrome's QNH; under a TMA or CTA, the QNH of an aerodrome beneath it.

quiz.q: Since when has the UK used hectopascals instead of millibars?
quiz.why: Hectopascals replaced millibars in the UK on 17 November 2011. 1 hPa = 1 mb, so the numbers are the same.
